value: after 48 h of feeding by 15 fourth-instar gypsy moth (Lymantria dispar) caterpillars, black poplar emitted far more of most volatiles than undamaged trees: cyclic monoterpenes about 2-fold, but acyclic monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes and the homoterpene DMNT many-fold (about 7000-fold for (E)-beta-ocimene, 4000-fold for DMNT, 250-fold for (E)-beta-caryophyllene); green leaf volatiles such as (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate rose rapidly at the onset of feeding and fell after the caterpillars were removed, aldoximes were induced immediately, salicyl aldehyde from near the onset, benzyl alcohol and benzene ethanol more slowly, and terpenoids kept being emitted for hours after removal, some until the end of the 96 h record; caterpillar species identity changed emission only slightly (only (E)-beta-caryophyllene, 3-methylbutyraldoxime, myrcene and nerolidol differed between Lymantria dispar and Laothoe populi fifth instars), while DMNT, benzyl alcohol and benzene ethanol were unaffected by herbivore identity or developmental stage
method: young trees grown from stem cuttings of old-growth trees (about 40 cm tall, 2 months old in the temporal experiment); volatiles collected in 6 h intervals over 96 h, herbivory 48 h; a second experiment compared control, second-instar and fifth-instar L. dispar, fifth-instar L. populi and a mixed group
conditions: 10 trees per treatment (herbivory and control) in the temporal experiment, 5 trees per treatment in the five-treatment species and stage experiment; the abstract also reports that early-instar L. dispar induced more nitrogenous volatiles and terpenoids than late instars, while DMNT was unaffected by stage; the paper does not name a cultivar and does not say the trees were one clone; no individual compound met all the criteria the authors set for a reliable enemy cue; herbivore-induced emission of the plant's own volatiles, the parasitoid-cue argument is the authors' discussion and was not tested

value: green leaf volatiles such as (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate were released both day and night with greater emission by day; terpenoid emission was also greater by day than at night, the day excess being much higher in light than dark (no fold given); benzyl cyanide and indole were emitted 2-3-fold more by day; benzene ethanol and benzyl alcohol were biphasic (high by day, reduced at night); 2-methylbutyraldoxime was not influenced by the light or dark period and salicyl aldehyde was emitted both day and night
method: volatiles of herbivore-damaged (gypsy moth) black poplar collected in 6 h intervals over 96 h, first collection starting at 5 pm with 3 h of light remaining
conditions: 10 trees per treatment in the temporal experiment, herbivory 48 h; the Discussion says some green leaf volatiles followed a pattern independent of light and dark without naming which; clock times of the peak per compound are not in the sentences read; trees about 40 cm tall and 2 months old

value: three Spodoptera littoralis caterpillars feeding 24 h on a red clover plant raised its total volatile emission three-fold over the undamaged control, with five compounds increased (1-octen-3-ol, (E)-beta-ocimene, (Z)-beta-ocimene, (E)-beta-caryophyllene, DMNT) and monoterpenes showing the largest relative rise; the number of volatiles did not change with herbivory; methyl salicylate was not detected; at the whole-community level only DMNT rose with herbivory in the Results (the Discussion adds (E)-beta-caryophyllene), and there were no significant interactions between herbivory and species richness, composition or identity
method: red clover grown alone or with Geranium pratense and/or Dactylis glomerata neighbours in pots, with or without three S. littoralis caterpillars on one focal plant (fed 24 h before 1 h headspace sampling); six randomised blocks, 48 pots
conditions: the figure legends give n = 6 and the table legends n = 5 per cell; neighbour identity changed red clover emission (highest with D. glomerata, G. pratense had no influence); seeds from a commercial supplier with no cultivar named; the effect of herbivory is one comparison within a study whose main finding is the neighbour effect; the baseline sentence quoted is the study's own Results statement
